s0101.literal: In the second year of Chengsheng of Liang, [Lang] led more than ten thousand households of his following across the Yangzi, entered Xuancheng commandery territory, and established a camp.
s0101.idiomatic: In Liang Chengsheng year two, Lang led more than ten thousand follower households across the Yangzi, entered Xuancheng commandery, and set up camp.

s0102.literal: Emperor Yuan of Liang appointed Lang Bearer of the Staff, Courier Direct-Communication Scattered-Cavalry Regular Attendant, Pacifying-South General, Area Commander over Military Affairs in South Yanzhou, and Inspector of South Yanzhou.
s0102.idiomatic: Emperor Yuan of Liang made Lang bearer of the staff, courier direct-communication scattered-cavalry regular attendant, pacifying-south general, commander of South Yanzhou armies, and inspector of the province.

s0103.literal: Before he took up the post, Jingzhou fell.
s0103.idiomatic: Before he could take up the post, Jingzhou fell.

s0105.literal: Fa Shang in youth was unrestrained and bold, possessed civil and military capacity and strategy; he began his career as magistrate of Jiangning and inherited enfeoffment as Marquis of Xingning county.
s0105.idiomatic: Fa Shang as a youth was bold and enterprising, with both civil and military talent; he began as magistrate of Jiangning and inherited the marquisate of Xingning.

s0106.literal: In the fifth year of Taijian he followed Wu Mingche on the northern campaign.
s0106.idiomatic: In Taijian year five he joined Wu Mingche's northern campaign.

s0107.literal: Soon he was given Courier Direct-Communication Scattered-Cavalry Gentleman, dismissed as magistrate of Jing, and successively served as Administrator of Liang and Ancheng.
s0107.idiomatic: He was soon made courier direct-communication scattered-cavalry gentleman, relieved as magistrate of Jing, and served in turn as administrator of Liang and Ancheng.

s0108.literal: In the Zhenming era he was made Area Commander over Military Affairs in the three prefectures of Ying, Ba, and Wu, and Inspector of Yingzhou.
s0108.idiomatic: During Zhenming he was made commander of armies in Ying, Ba, and Wu and inspector of Yingzhou.

s0109.literal: When Sui forces crossed the Yangzi, Fa Shang surrendered to the Prince of Qin, commander of the Handong route.
s0109.idiomatic: When the Sui army crossed the Yangzi, Fa Shang surrendered to the Prince of Qin, commander on the Handong route.

s0110.literal: Entering Sui service, he successively was Inspector of the four prefectures Shao, Guan, Mian, and Feng, and Administrator of the two commanderies Badong and Dunhuang.
s0110.idiomatic: Under the Sui he served in turn as inspector of Shao, Guan, Mian, and Feng and as administrator of Badong and Dunhuang.

s0111.literal: Zhou Jiong, style name Wenzhao, was a native of Ancheng in Ruyang.
s0111.idiomatic: Zhou Jiong, courtesy name Wenzhao, was from Ancheng in Ruyang.

s0112.literal: His grandfather Qiang was Qi Crown Prince's Household Attendant and Inspector of Liangzhou.
s0112.idiomatic: His grandfather Qiang had been crown prince's household attendant under Qi and inspector of Liangzhou.

s0113.literal: His father Lingqi was Liang Courier Direct-Communication Scattered-Cavalry Regular Attendant and Inspector of the two prefectures Lu and Gui, Marquis of Baocheng county.
s0113.idiomatic: His father Lingqi was Liang courier direct-communication scattered-cavalry regular attendant and inspector of Lu and Gui, marquis of Baocheng county.

s0114.literal: When the Founder took the throne, Wang Lin held the upper Yangzi; Jiong followed him with his prefecture.
s0114.idiomatic: When the Founder took the throne, Wang Lin held the upper Yangzi, and Jiong brought his province to his side.

s0115.literal: When Wang Lin sent his generals Cao Qing and others to attack Zhou Di, he also had Jiong lead troops in pincer advance; [Jiong] was defeated by Hou Andu, captured, and sent to the capital.
s0115.idiomatic: When Wang Lin sent Cao Qing and others against Zhou Di, he also ordered Jiong to advance in concert; Hou Andu defeated him, took him prisoner, and sent him to court.

s0116.literal: Emperor Wen released Jiong and appointed him Martial-Power General and Inspector of Dingzhou, concurrently Administrator of the two commanderies Xiyang and Wuchang.
s0116.idiomatic: Emperor Wen freed Jiong and made him martial-power general and inspector of Dingzhou, with concurrent charge of Xiyang and Wuchang.

s0117.literal: In the second year of Tianjia, Liu Yi held Dongyang in rebellion; Emperor Wen summoned Jiong back to the capital, intending to have him campaign against Yi.
s0117.idiomatic: In Tianjia year two Liu Yi rebelled at Dongyang; Emperor Wen recalled Jiong to the capital to lead the campaign against him.

s0118.literal: Before he arrived, Yi was pacified; Jiong returned to his original command.
s0118.idiomatic: Before he arrived, Yi had been suppressed, and Jiong returned to his post.

s0119.literal: In the first year of Tiankang he shared in the merit of pacifying Hua Jiao and was given Supernumerary Scattered-Cavalry Regular Attendant.
s0119.idiomatic: In Tiankang year one he shared credit for suppressing Hua Jiao and was made supernumerary scattered-cavalry regular attendant.

s0120.literal: In the first year of Taijian he was transferred to Bearer of the Staff, Dragon-Prancing General, and Courier Direct-Communication Scattered-Cavalry Regular Attendant.
s0120.idiomatic: In Taijian year one he was made bearer of the staff, dragon-prancing general, and courier direct-communication scattered-cavalry regular attendant.

s0121.literal: In year five he was advanced to Bearer of the Staff with full credentials, Western Route Area Commander over Military Affairs in the six prefectures An, Qi, Jiang, Heng, Si, and Ding, and Inspector of Anzhou; his enfeoffment was changed to Marquis of Longyuan county, fief increased together with the former to one thousand households.
s0121.idiomatic: In year five he was promoted to full bearer of the staff, western-route commander of armies in An, Qi, Jiang, Heng, Si, and Ding, and inspector of Anzhou; his title was changed to marquis of Longyuan, with fief raised to one thousand households in all.

s0122.literal: That year he followed Area Commander Wu Mingche on the northern campaign; wherever he went he was victorious, and within one month he took twelve cities.
s0122.idiomatic: That year he followed Wu Mingche north; he carried every assault and took twelve cities in a month.

s0123.literal: Qi sent Left Assistant in the Department of State Affairs Lu Qian with twenty thousand men out from Ba and Qi; he encountered Jiong.
s0123.idiomatic: Qi sent Lu Qian, left assistant in the department of state affairs, with twenty thousand men from Ba and Qi, and he met Jiong.

s0124.literal: Jiong left the weak and the baggage train, set decoy troops to face them, and personally led picked warriors by a bypath to strike their rear; he inflicted a great defeat on Qian's army and captured weapons, horses, and mules beyond counting.
s0124.idiomatic: Jiong left the weak and the baggage, posted decoys to hold them, and led picked men by a hidden route to strike their rear; he routed Qian's army and seized arms, horses, and mules beyond count.

s0125.literal: He advanced to attack Bazhou and took it.
s0125.idiomatic: He then attacked and captured Bazhou.

s0126.literal: Thereupon the cities north of the Yangzi and the gentry and people of Guyang all executed their chieftains and surrendered their cities.
s0126.idiomatic: Then the cities north of the river and the people of Guyang killed their leaders and surrendered.

s0127.literal: His title was advanced to General Who Harmonizes with the Rong and Scattered-Cavalry Regular Attendant; fief increased together with the former to one thousand five hundred households.
s0127.idiomatic: He was promoted to general who harmonizes with the Rong and scattered-cavalry regular attendant, with fief raised to one thousand five hundred households in all.

s0128.literal: An edict then recalled Jiong to court.
s0128.idiomatic: An edict then recalled him to court.

s0129.literal: Earlier, Xiao Cha's Inspector of Dingzhou Tian Longsheng had surrendered his city;
s0129.idiomatic: Earlier Tian Longsheng, inspector of Dingzhou under Xiao Cha, had surrendered his city;

s0130.literal: when Jiong entered court, Longsheng rebelled with the six prefectures and seven garrisons north of the Yangzi and went over to Qi; Qi sent the Prince of Liyang, Gao Jing'an, to lead troops to support him.
s0130.idiomatic: but when Jiong came to court, Longsheng rebelled with six prefectures and seven garrisons north of the river and defected to Qi, which sent Prince Jing'an of Liyang with an army to aid him.

s0131.literal: Thereupon [the court] made Jiong Grand Commander of the Northern Yangzi Route, commanding all armies, to campaign against Longsheng.
s0131.idiomatic: The court then made Jiong grand commander on the northern Yangzi route and gave him all armies to crush Longsheng.

s0132.literal: Longsheng sent Yiyang Administrator Tian Longyan with twenty thousand men to form battle lines at Tingchuan; Gao Jing'an at Shuiling and Yinshan gave him vocal support; Longsheng led troops to encamp separately in the valleys.
s0132.idiomatic: Longsheng sent Tian Longyan, administrator of Yiyang, with twenty thousand men to line up at Tingchuan; Gao Jing'an backed him from Shuiling and Yinshan; Longsheng camped apart in the hills.

s0133.literal: Jiong then divided his troops to face each army, personally led his champions in the first strike on Longsheng, and inflicted a great defeat; Longyan fled at the sight of dust and both were pursued and beheaded; Gao Jing'an fled; he fully recovered the territory north of the Yangzi.
s0133.idiomatic: Jiong split his force to hold each enemy host, led his champions in a first blow on Longsheng, and routed him; Longyan fled at the dust and both were run down and killed; Gao Jing'an escaped; and the whole north bank was recovered.

s0134.literal: For merit fief was increased together with the former to two thousand households; his title was advanced to General Who Pacifies the North, Inspector of Dingzhou, bearer of the staff and area command unchanged; he was also granted a troupe of female entertainers.
s0134.idiomatic: For merit his fief rose to two thousand households in all; he was made general who pacifies the north and inspector of Dingzhou, keeping staff and command; and he received a troupe of female entertainers.

s0135.literal: In the eighth year of Taijian he died in office, aged sixty-four.
s0135.idiomatic: In Taijian year eight he died in office at sixty-four.

s0136.literal: Posthumously he was given Inspector of Sizhou, enfeoffed as Duke of Wuchang commandery, posthumous name Zhuang.
s0136.idiomatic: He was posthumously made inspector of Sizhou and duke of Wuchang commandery, with the posthumous name Zhuang.

s0137.literal: His son Faseng succeeded him and reached the post of Administrator of Xuancheng.
s0137.idiomatic: His son Faseng succeeded him and rose to administrator of Xuancheng.

s0138.literal: The historiographer says: Those several men either galloped through earlier ages or held their native districts; all recognized the turn of fortune, attached themselves as opportunity arose, rose to rank as regional governors, and enfeoffment reached full marquis—magnificent indeed.
s0138.idiomatic: The historiographer writes: These men either rode the currents of an earlier age or held their home country; each saw where fortune was turning, joined at the right moment, rose to govern provinces, and won marquisates—how splendid.

s0139.literal: Formerly Zhang Er and Chen Yu were as close as the nearest kin; Zhou Fu and Zhou Di likewise swore bonds like intimate relatives—yet soon they turned blades and slaughtered one another; this was even more extreme than Hu and Yue.
s0139.idiomatic: Once Zhang Er and Chen Yu stood as close as kin; Zhou Fu and Zhou Di swore the same kind of bond—yet they soon drew blades on each other, a breach worse than between Hu and Yue.

s0140.literal: Enmity arose from power and profit—how base!
s0140.idiomatic: Their feud grew from rank and gain—how base!

s0142.literal: Again defeated Hou Jing's general Hou Zijian at Hushu—Comment: "Hushu" should read "Gudu."
s0142.idiomatic: On again defeating Hou Jing's general Hou Zijian at Hushu: Hushu should read Gudu.

s0143.literal: In the first year of Chengsheng of Liang, Wang Sengbian and others defeated Hou Jing's general Hou Zijian at Gudu—see the Liang History biography of Hou Jing and the Comprehensive Mirror.
s0143.idiomatic: In Liang Chengsheng year one Wang Sengbian and others defeated Hou Zijian at Gudu; see the Liang History biography of Hou Jing and the Comprehensive Mirror.

s0145.literal: [Concurrently] Administrator of Hedong—changed according to the History of the Southern Dynasties.
s0145.idiomatic: [Concurrently] administrator of Hedong—emended per the History of the Southern Dynasties.

s0146.literal: Comment: Qian Daxin's Examination of Discrepancies in the Twenty-Two Histories says: "'zhen' should read 'ling.'
s0146.idiomatic: Note: Qian Daxin writes in his Examination of Discrepancies in the Twenty-Two Histories: zhen should read ling.

s0147.literal: Between Liang and Chen it was common for men to hold the salary of inspector while concurrently serving as commandery administrator or county magistrate."
s0147.idiomatic: Between Liang and Chen it was common to hold inspector's salary while concurrently governing a commandery or county."

s0150.literal: [Islet]—changed according to the History of the Southern Dynasties.
s0150.idiomatic: [Islet]—emended per the History of the Southern Dynasties.

s0151.literal: Comment: Essentials of Historical Geography 78 says that in Jiangling county of Jingzhou prefecture there was Long Islet, in the river sixteen li southwest of the prefectural seat.
s0151.idiomatic: Note: Essentials of Historical Geography 78 places Long Islet in the river sixteen li southwest of Jiangling, seat of Jingzhou.

s0152.literal: Where Liu Yi, Yu Xiaoshou, Zhou Di, and others were rising in force—"rising in force" in all editions reads "swarming like bees"; the History of the Southern Dynasties and Yuan Gui 412 the same.
s0152.idiomatic: On Liu Yi, Yu Xiaoshou, Zhou Di, and others rising in force: every edition reads swarming like bees; the History of the Southern Dynasties and Yuan Gui 412 agree.

s0153.literal: Comment: "rising in force" means all rising at once with sharp, irresistible momentum.
s0153.idiomatic: Note: rising in force means erupting together with irresistible sharpness.

s0154.literal: In ancient books "rising in force" and "swarming like bees" often interchange, as in the Later Han Annals of Emperor Guangwu, "bandits rose in force," commentary: "the character 'force' is sometimes written 'bee'"—that is the pattern.
s0154.idiomatic: Ancient texts often alternate rising in force and swarming like bees, as in the Later Han Annals of Guangwu: bandits rose in force, with a note that force may be written bee—that is the pattern.

s0155.literal: Qi sent Mobile Headquarters Murong Shaozong with thirty thousand men to attack the garrisons at Yugou—Qian Daxin's Examination of Discrepancies in the Twenty-Two Histories says: "Comment: Murong Shaozong died before Qi received the mandate; how could he still be alive at this time?
s0155.idiomatic: On Qi sending Murong Shaozong with thirty thousand men against Yugou: Qian Daxin notes that Shaozong died before Qi received the mandate and could not have been alive here.

s0156.literal: This is an error of transmitted report in the historians; the History of the Southern Dynasties also kept the old report and did not correct it by the Northern History."
s0156.idiomatic: This is a transmitted error; the History of the Southern Dynasties kept the old tale and did not correct it against the Northern History."

s0157.literal: Liang Interior Secretary and Prince of Shixing Xiao Yi yielded the commandery to Zhou Xu—Qian Daxin's Examination of Discrepancies in the Twenty-Two Histories says: "Comment: According to the Liang History and the History of the Southern Dynasties, when Prince Shixing Xiao Dan died his heir Liang succeeded; there is no one named 'Yi.'
s0157.idiomatic: On Liang interior secretary and Prince of Shixing Xiao Yi yielding the commandery to Zhou Xu: Qian Daxin notes that the Liang History and History of the Southern Dynasties show Prince Shixing Xiao Dan succeeded by his heir Liang, with no Yi.

s0158.literal: " Zhang Senkai's collation note also says: "Prince Shixing Xiao Dan's heir Liang was still alive at the time; it does not say his name was Yi; it is unknown who Yi was to Dan."
s0158.idiomatic: Zhang Senkai adds: Prince Shixing Xiao Dan's heir Liang was still alive; the text never names Yi; who Yi was to Dan is unknown."

s0159.literal: Yu Xiaoshou and Wang Lin's partisan Li
s0159.idiomatic: Yu Xiaoshou and Wang Lin's partisan Li

s0161.literal: [Xiao] Qin and others jointly besieged Zhou Di—changed according to the History of the Southern Dynasties.
s0161.idiomatic: [Xiao] Qin and others jointly besieged Zhou Di—emended per the History of the Southern Dynasties.

s0166.literal: , and the Northern Qi History biography of Wang Lin all read "Li Xiaoqin."
s0166.idiomatic: , the biography of Zhou Di, and the Northern Qi History biography of Wang Lin all read Li Xiaoqin.

s0167.literal: Granted a troupe of female music—"music" in all editions reads "courtesans."
s0167.idiomatic: On granted a troupe of female music: every edition reads courtesans for music.

s0168.literal: The two characters "one troupe" were originally missing and are supplied from the editions.
s0168.idiomatic: The words "one troupe" were missing in the base text and are restored from other editions.

s0169.literal: Thus brought death upon himself—"upon himself" was originally written "ten"; a block-print error; now corrected according to Yuan Gui 452 and 595.
s0169.idiomatic: On "thus brought death upon himself": "upon himself" was originally written ten, a carving error; emended per Yuan Gui 452 and 595.

s0170.literal: According to the Northern Supervisory, Ji, and Palace editions, "upon himself" (pu) was written "body" (shen); probably a later mistaken change.
s0170.idiomatic: According to the Northern Supervisory, Ji, and Palace editions, pu (upon himself) was written shen (body); probably a later mistaken change.
